name: Silicone scar tape

lead: Silicone scar tape, or silicone gel sheeting, is a thin adhesive sheet worn over a healing or healed scar. People use it mainly to flatten and soften raised hypertrophic and keloid scars so they show less, and it is sold over the counter for surgical and acne scars.

Silicone is thought to hydrate the outer skin layer and occlude the scar, which calms fibroblast activity and collagen overproduction; light pressure and temperature effects may also play a part, and the exact mechanism is not established. It is one of the more widely recommended topical scar products. Cochrane reviews describe the trials as generally weak, with some data suggesting benefit in scar-prone people.

paras: Sheets are cut to size and worn over the scar for many hours a day, often overnight, over a period of months. They are washed and reused, and people typically start once the wound has closed.

Side effects are mainly rashes, itching, or maceration under the sheet, and it should not go on open wounds. The 2013 Cochrane review judged most trials to be of poor quality, so improvement may be modest and slow. It is not reported to remove a mature, flat scar.

web.title: Silicone gel sheeting for treating hypertrophic scars (protocol)

angle.text: Users wear the sheets over raised or keloid scars, and sometimes other marks, so the scar flattens and fades over months. The sheet hydrates and occludes the scar, which tones down collagen overproduction; it has been studied for hypertrophic and keloid scars, while use on acne scars is mostly anecdotal.

lead: Silicone scar tape, also called silicone gel sheeting, is a thin, soft, self-adhesive sheet of medical-grade silicone worn over a healed scar. People use it to make raised, red or thickened scars flatter, softer and less noticeable, including surgical scars, burn scars and acne-area scars on the face and body. It is sold over the counter as strips, sheets and shaped patches, and is washable and reusable.[1][2]

A typical course described in the Cochrane protocol is 8 to 12 weeks, with sheets worn for many hours a day and up to 24 hours, removed for washing.[2] Silicone products are, according to Wikipedia, widely used both to prevent scarring and to improve existing scars, although a Cochrane review found only weak evidence for prevention and the included studies were of poor quality and prone to bias.[1][3]

The approach is aimed at raised scars, which are more common in darker skin and in wounds under tension, rather than at flat, mature scars. Reported hypertrophic scar prevalence ranges from 32 to 72 percent, with 40 to 70 percent after surgery and up to 91 percent after burns.[2]

paras: A scar is an area of fibrous tissue that replaces normal skin after injury. Scar collagen is arranged differently from that in normal skin, with cross-linked, aligned fibres, and skin scars lack sweat glands and hair follicles [1]. Hypertrophic scars are raised above the surrounding skin, typically appear within about 4 to 8 weeks after wound closure and stay within the wound boundary, whereas keloids can extend beyond the original wound and are more common in people with darker skin. Atrophic scars are sunken, often after acne [1]. Grokipedia, an AI-generated encyclopedia, says most scars fade over up to two years or more but cannot be completely removed, and that early redness fades as the scar matures [4].

The sheets are flexible silicone, usually self-adhesive and often reusable after washing. They are applied over closed skin, not open wounds. In the Wikipedia overview of scar treatment, silicone sheeting appears in the dressings and topical silicone category alongside pressure dressings, which are common in burn and hypertrophic scar management though supporting evidence is described as lacking [1]. Other approaches listed there include chemical peels, fillers, lasers, steroid injections, surgical revision, massage and radiotherapy, each with varying evidence [1].

Hypertrophic scars usually appear within about 4 to 8 weeks of wound closure and often regress within about a year, while keloids extend beyond the wound edges and do not regress, which is why the Cochrane programme assesses them separately.[1][2] Redness after injury usually fades but can take years in severe cases.[1]

Among other scar options Wikipedia lists long-term corticosteroid injections for flattening keloids and hypertrophic scars, nonablative lasers, low-dose superficial radiotherapy for recurrence prevention in severe cases, and surgery, whose recurrence rate for keloid excision alone is described as near 45 percent and which is usually combined with pressure or silicone.[1]

The mechanism is not fully established. The Cochrane protocol describes occlusion and hydration of the outer epidermis, since the sheets reduce water evaporation from the skin, as the leading explanation, and suggests that a small rise in skin surface temperature may increase collagenase activity. The protocol states that the effect is not believed to come from pressure or altered oxygen tension, and that scar biopsies showed no foreign body reaction.[2]

Other accounts mention mild pressure effects, and Wikipedia notes more generally that mechanical stress on a wound can stimulate scarring and that reducing stress has been linked to smaller scars.[1] Silicone products differ from pressure garments, which are commonly used for burn and hypertrophic scars even though supporting trials are limited.[1]

The principal evidence is the Cochrane systematic review Silicone gel sheeting for preventing and treating hypertrophic and keloid scars, published in 2013 by O'Brien and colleagues. It pooled hypertrophic and keloid scars; Wikipedia summarises it as finding weak evidence that silicone gel sheeting helps prevent scarring, with studies of poor quality and susceptible to bias.[1][3] The 2019 protocol describing a follow-up review characterises the earlier review as noting a lack of robust evidence, low participant numbers and inadequate follow-up, and describes a 2017 review as having similar weaknesses.[2]

The 2019 protocol sets out plans to split the earlier combined review into separate treatment and prevention reviews for each scar type, starting with silicone gel sheeting as treatment for hypertrophic scars compared with standard care or other therapies.[2]

Wikipedia also reports a study from the Catholic University of Korea concluding that verapamil-releasing silicone gel reduced scar height and redness in a hypertrophic scar model compared with conventional silicone gel. This concerns a different, experimental product.[1]

A 2024 laboratory study incorporated antimicrobial ceragenins into silicone- and polyacrylate-based medical adhesives and scar-tape adhesives to reduce microbial colonisation, reporting reduced microbial growth over weeks and no dermal irritation in an in vivo model. It was a materials study and did not evaluate scar appearance.[5]

Side effects described for silicone sheeting are mainly itching, rash and skin maceration under the sheet, and the sheets are applied over closed skin rather than open wounds.[3][2] The review authors' judgement that trials were of poor quality means improvement estimates are uncertain.[1][3] Wikipedia lists other scar treatments with their own risks, such as filler reactions and cautions about peels in darker skin and keloid-prone people.[1]

Silicone scar sheets are listed in the body-care shelf as a low-cost option for raised scars, including acne and surgical scars. No looksmaxxing forum thread collected for this entry discusses silicone sheeting, so no community-specific protocols or claims are documented here.
